chapter_title: Designing an A/B Test with Students
learning_objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight sentences from draft consent letters is acceptable or a problem, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** consent-letter-checker
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate
**Bloom Verb:** judge
**Learning Objective:** The learner will judge whether each of eight sentences from draft consent letters is acceptable or a problem, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** Informed Consent, Sampling Bias (both defined in this chapter above this block). **Evidence of Mastery:** For each sentence the learner commits one of two bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the consent parts is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) A promise of a better grade encourages participation. (2) Participation can be required if the activity is part of class. (3) More data is always better. **Instructional Rationale:** Judging a sentence against the parts of valid consent is an Evaluate-level action. Sentences that pressure, over-collect, or over-share, mixed with sound ones, teach the learner what a letter must and must not say. **Content:** The two bins: Acceptable, and Problem. The eight sentences (all made up, for the Watershed Basics pilot): | # | Sentence from a draft letter | Correct bin | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Your child will use one of two versions of a lesson on watersheds, and a computer will choose which version by chance. | Acceptable | It states what students do and that assignment is random. | | 2 | Taking part will raise your child's science grade. | Problem | It promises a benefit that the test cannot promise, and it ties participation to the grade. | | 3 | Taking part is voluntary. Your child may stop at any time, and nothing will happen to their grade. | Acceptable | It states that participation is voluntary and withdrawal is free. | | 4 | All students must take part, and those who decline will lose participation points. | Problem | It forces participation and penalizes refusal. | | 5 | We will collect your child's name, birthdate, home address, and phone number with every test. | Problem | It collects personal information that the test does not need. | | 6 | Scores are stored under a code number. Names are kept in a separate locked file that only the teacher can open, and the file will be deleted on 2027-06-30. | Acceptable | It states how data is protected and when it is deleted. | | 7 | Results may be shared with any company that wants them. | Problem | It allows unlimited sharing of student information. | | 8 | Questions about the test may be sent to the teacher at the school office or to the district research contact. | Acceptable | It gives a way to reach a person. | **Provenance:** The sentences are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The consent parts follow the chapter section "Informed Consent". The sim adds the note "check your school's rules". **Rules:** Each sentence has exactly one correct bin, four per bin. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees one sentence and the two bins, and may open the table of consent parts. Opening it does not change the score. 2. The learner places the sentence in a bin, and the placement is committed. 3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text. 4. After sentence 8 the sim shows the summary. **Feedback:** 8 sentences in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can read a consent letter critically." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed sentence. **Starting State:** The first sentence in the shuffled order and the two bins. The question shown is "Does this sentence belong in a good consent letter?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter's table of consent parts and its three practical rules are the basis of the sentences.
